title: Milk that turns slowly (69–75)
hookLine: an evil deed, like fresh milk, does not turn at once; it smolders like fire under ash

lines: MILK IN A PAIL ON THE COUNTER.
FINE AT LUNCH. FINE BY EVENING.
cards: Before refrigerators, milk came straight from the cow into a pail. Leave it on the counter and nothing happened right away. It looked fine.
It smelled fine at lunch, maybe still fine by evening. Then, the next morning, it had turned: sour, thick, undrinkable. The change was happening the whole time.
You just couldn't see it yet. A lot of life works that way: a small lie, a shortcut, a harsh word that seemed to cost nothing, until one day it did.

teach.h: SWEET AS HONEY, UNTIL IT RIPENS.
teach.b: Verse sixty-nine, in Müller's English: “As long as the evil deed done does not bear fruit, the fool thinks it is like honey; but when it ripens, then the fool suffers grief.”
Like honey: the shortcut feels sweet, because nothing has happened yet.

teach.h: MILK THAT DOESN'T TURN AT ONCE.
teach.b: Then verse seventy-one: “An evil deed, like newly-drawn milk, does not turn (suddenly); smouldering, like fire covered by ashes, it follows the fool.” Two pictures. Fresh milk that sours slowly.
And a fire banked under ash: the surface gray and cool-looking, the coals underneath still hot, waiting for a careless foot. This is the Buddhist teaching of kamma at its most down-to-earth.
Actions have results, but the results often ripen slowly, and that delay is exactly what fools us. The delay isn't proof that nothing happened. It's just the milk, still on the counter.
The rest of the chapter warns about something just as quiet: knowledge used for the wrong ends, and wanting a reputation, the best seat, authority over others.
Then it ends with a verse many people carry for life, verse seventy-five: “One is the road that leads to wealth, another the road that leads to Nirvana.” Not a condemnation of earning a living.
A reminder that the two roads point in different directions, and a person should know which one they're walking. So chapter five, the fool, closes. Long is the night, bala.
Wise so far. Taste the soup.
And now: it turns slowly. Which is also good news. Good deeds ripen slowly too.

how: Buddhist teachers use the milk and ash verses to explain kamma: actions have results, but those results may ripen slowly, which is why small harmful acts are taken seriously.

o: milk, which turns sour slowly, not all at once
butter churned from milk for a temple lamp
a cloth bag for carrying a monk's bowl

games.q: match the pictures in verses sixty-nine to seventy-five.
p: how the deed feels before it ripens
one to wealth, one to nibbana

s: if nothing bad happens right away, the deed had no result
verse seventy-one says it turns slowly, like milk or fire under ash.
verse seventy-five contrasts the road to wealth with the road to nibbana
a reminder to know which road you're on.
the fool chapter warns against wanting reputation and the best seat
verses seventy-three and seventy-four describe it.

games.q: you cut a small corner at work. a week passes; nobody noticed. what does verse sixty-nine say the fool thinks?
o: that it was wrong and should be fixed.
that it's sweet as honey, since nothing has happened.
games.why: the fool thinks it is like honey, until it ripens. the verse's point is the delay, not the absence of results.

practice: Let one slow consequence from your own life come to mind: something you did long ago that only caught up with you later, or a good habit that took months to show its fruit, a friendship tended, a skill practiced, a kindness that came back.
Notice the gap between the deed and the result. Then look gently at today, without judgment: is anything sitting on the counter that you might want to deal with before it turns?

wordCard.voice: Khira. Milk: an action's results ripening late, like fresh milk souring, or fire hidden under ash.

orig.note: Pali: milk, from verse seventy-one: 'sajju khiramva muccati,' like fresh milk, it doesn't turn at once.

carryVoice: Your line: it turns slowly. Bitter or sweet, the delay isn't the end of it. Chapter five, closed.
